analysis.one_liner: Suspend endangered-species protections for the spotted owl for five years while allowing federal old-growth logging.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it sat in three House committees for over a year, got one subcommittee hearing, and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have suspended the part of the Endangered Species Act that requires federal agencies to avoid harming an endangered species' habitat. For five years, timber sales — including road building — on national forest lands in the Pacific Northwest could have gone ahead even if they destroyed Northern Spotted Owl habitat, while the Agriculture Department studied whether the owl was actually threatened. The owl's habitat is old-growth forest, so any logging sales during the exemption would have permanently removed the very habitat under study.
analysis.who_benefits: The timber industry would gain five years of unrestricted access to roughly 5 billion board feet a year of old-growth federal timber in Oregon and Washington without endangered-species review. Timber-dependent towns would keep jobs tied to federal timber sales for the study period — the bill's findings claim protecting the owl could cost 100,000 to 160,000 jobs and eventually 34,000 in Oregon and Washington.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The timber industry and logging towns

how_it_helps.text: For five years, timber sales, road construction, and related activities on National Forest System lands would be exempt from the Endangered Species Act requirement that federal agencies avoid jeopardizing the spotted owl or its habitat [S2][S3].

The bill's findings argue that old-growth national forests supply about 5 billion board feet of timber annually and that owl protections could put up to 2.6 million acres off-limits, costing an estimated 100,000 to 160,000 jobs in the short term and 34,000 long term in Oregon and Washington [S3].
The bill directs the Secretary of Agriculture to study the owl's range and habitat needs, including whether it can survive in non-old-growth stands, and report back within five years [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Northern Spotted Owl and the public that owns the national forests. Old-growth logged during the five-year exemption cannot be restored on any human timescale, so habitat destroyed while the study ran would be gone before the science was settled. Future timber supply would also shrink, since the bill's own findings note most remaining old-growth is already the only timber base left.
analysis.who_pays_short: The spotted owl and the public's old-growth forests

drawbacks.text: The exemption removes the only legal check — the Endangered Species Act's requirement that agencies avoid jeopardizing the owl — during the exact period when its fate would be decided [S2][S3].

The bill's own findings say about 92 percent of the owl's habitat is old-growth and mature forest on federal lands in Oregon, Washington, and California, meaning five years of unrestricted sales could permanently destroy the habitat being studied [S3].

The study premise cuts both ways: the bill questions the science behind the owl's decline (arguing radio transmitters raised owl mortality and that surveys ignored non-old-growth stands), but a five-year logging window while the question is studied risks a decision that cannot be undone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a real, near-term economic stake — jobs in timber towns, as its own findings emphasize — for a five-year guarantee that logging could not be stopped on owl habitat. The cost is one-sided in time: timber jobs deferred can return or adjust, but old-growth forest and owl habitat logged during the exemption are gone permanently. A study could have been funded without suspending the species protections that were the reason for the study, which is why critics saw the exemption, not the research, as the bill's real purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to subcommittees, got a single subcommittee hearing in July 1990, was never reported out for a floor vote, and expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991 — by then the record simply pointed to a different bill.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert F. Smith (R-OR) introduced the bill on March 23, 1989, and it was referred jointly to the Agriculture, Interior and Insular Affairs, and Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committees [S1][S5].
It was sent to subcommittees in each committee in late March and April 1989, and executive comment was requested from USDA, Interior, and EPA [S5].
The only substantive action was a subcommittee hearing on July 24, 1990; no committee ever reported the bill to the House floor [S5].
On September 13, 1990, the record simply notes 'See H.R. 5295,' and the bill died with the Congress on January 3, 1991 [S5][S1].
It had 12 cosponsors — 11 Republicans and 1 Democrat, mostly members from timber states [S4][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The spotted owl and the public's remaining old-growth forests — no five-year logging exemption ever took effect. The timber industry, which sought a guaranteed five years of sales without species review, gained nothing from this bill, though the underlying fight over Northwest logging continued in other legislation.

for.name: Rep. Robert F. Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt spotted owl habitat from endangered-species review for five years and recruited additional sponsors.

for.name: 11 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (along with 1 House Democrat), nearly all from timber-region states.

for.name: Northwest timber industry
for.role: Forest products companies and logging interests
for.what_they_did: Backed legislation to keep federal old-growth timber flowing while the owl's status was studied.

against.name: House Agriculture, Interior and Insular Affairs, and Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committees
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill to the House floor; the only action in 16 months was one subcommittee hearing.

against.name: Conservation and environmental organizations
against.what_they_did: Opposed exempting the spotted owl from the Endangered Species Act, pushing instead for its listing as threatened.

against.name: Fish and Wildlife Service (George H.W. Bush administration)
against.what_they_did: Listed the Northern Spotted Owl as a threatened species in June 1990, giving legal protection independent of this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship came from the Republican side except one Democrat, with 11 of 12 cosponsors Republican — the bill never got far enough to produce a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have guaranteed five years of old-growth federal timber sales without endangered-species review, preserving roughly 5 billion board feet a year of supply by the bill's own accounting. The public cost was permanent loss of the owl's old-growth habitat on lands the public owns.

industries.industry: Timber-dependent logging communities in Oregon, Washington, and California
industries.note: The bill aimed to shield jobs tied to federal timber sales, citing potential losses of 100,000 to 160,000 positions if owl protections took effect. The same logging that protected those jobs short-term would have depleted the old-growth base those communities depend on long-term.

industries.industry: Recreation, fishing, and tourism economies tied to national forests
industries.note: Unrestricted logging and road construction on old-growth stands would have degraded the forest values these economies depend on. Their interests ran with protecting the owl's habitat.
